common_name: Zefa Fino Fennel (Bolt-Resistant Swiss Florence Fennel)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in mid- to late summer for a fall crop; Zefa Fino was bred at a Swiss federal research station specifically to resist the premature bolting that plagues most open-pollinated Florence fennel.

directions: Direct sow into rich, evenly moist soil since fennel forms a taproot and transplants poorly; Zefa Fino is the Swiss-bred workhorse behind much of the modern Florence fennel seed trade, prized for holding in the ground and resisting bolting far longer than older open-pollinated types even under fluctuating spring temperatures. Plants form large, dense, rounded white bulbs with a sweet, mild anise flavor and crisp texture that stays tender rather than turning pithy as the season progresses. Mound soil around the swelling base as the bulb develops to keep it pale and tender, and harvest once bulbs reach the size of a tennis ball to a fist before the plant sends up a flowering stalk.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow in spring once soil is workable, or sow in summer for a fall harvest; Mantovano was bred for spring sowing and shows strong resistance to bolting compared with older Italian fennel strains.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, evenly moist soil, since fennel resents root disturbance; Mantovano is a traditional Italian heirloom named for the Mantua region, valued for its large, flattened, very white bulbs and a sweeter, more assertively anise-forward flavor than many other Florence fennel strains. It matures earlier than most bulbing fennel and has an unusual habit of continuing to bulk up in the ground for weeks after reaching harvest size rather than splitting or turning woody, which gives growers real flexibility in harvest timing. Mound soil lightly around the base as the bulb swells to keep it pale, and use young bulbs raw in salads or slice and roast larger ones for a milder, caramelized flavor.
sources: Organic Seed Alliance / Northern Organic Vegetable Improvement Collaborative (NOVIC) variety trials

common_name: Gobbo di Nizza Cardoon (Piedmontese Heirloom Blanching Cardoon)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant into deep, rich soil once frost danger has passed; Gobbo di Nizza takes its name from the traditional Piedmontese practice of tipping plants over and burying the stalks in trenches in fall, which curves and blanches them into their signature hunchbacked shape.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gobbo di Nizza Monferrato is a heritage Piedmontese cardoon, listed by Slow Food's Ark of Taste, grown for its broad, fleshy, greeny-gray leaf ribs that carry relatively few strings and spines compared with wild cardoon. In late fall growers traditionally dig a shallow trench, lay the whole plant over into it, and bury the stalks in soil for several weeks, which both blanches the ribs pale and forces them into the curved, hunchbacked form that gives the variety its name. Blanched stalks are braised, fried, added to gratins, or eaten raw dipped in olive oil, and the fleshy root is edible as well, prepared much like a parsnip.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste

common_name: Gigante di Romagna Cardoon (Italian Large Nearly-Spineless Cardoon)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes into deep, richly amended soil; Gigante di Romagna is one of the largest cardoon strains grown, so give it ample room and generous feeding to reach full size.

directions: Start seed indoors and set transplants into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing generous space for its large mature footprint; Gigante di Romagna is a heirloom Italian cardoon from the Romagna region prized for producing unusually thick, wide, nearly spineless leaf ribs that are easier and less prickly to handle at harvest than most other cardoon strains. As with other cardoons, the coarse, bitter raw ribs are transformed by blanching, achieved by wrapping the mature plant in cardboard, burlap, or straw for three to four weeks before harvest to exclude light and mellow the flavor. The blanched ribs are classically braised, breaded and fried, or baked into a gratin, and the plant's tall, silvery, deeply cut foliage and thistle-like purple flower heads make it a dramatic architectural presence in the garden even where it is not harvested.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Mediterranean Vegetable Crops

common_name: Giant Pascal Celery (Classic French Heirloom Winter Celery)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-12 weeks before last frost, since celery seed is slow to germinate and seedlings grow slowly at first; transplant into rich, consistently moist soil after frost danger passes, or start in mid-summer for a fall and winter storage crop.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into very fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Giant Pascal, also sold as Giant Golden Pascal, is a French-derived heirloom celery documented in American seed catalogs since the late nineteenth century and long regarded as the standard for winter keeping. Its stalks grow notably thick and full-bodied, with a rich, nutty flavor that many gardeners find fuller than modern hybrid celery, and the ribs stay crisp and remarkably tolerant of cool fall and winter conditions. Blanch by tying the outer stalks together and mounding soil or wrapping paper around the base of the plant for two to three weeks before harvest, which lightens the green color to gold and softens any bitterness. Because it stores and holds in the garden well into winter, Giant Pascal has traditionally been the go-to celery for late-season harvest and root-cellar storage.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company historical seed catalogs
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: Golden Self-Blanching Celery (1883 Naturally-Blanching Heirloom Celery)

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since celery seed germinates slowly and can take up to three weeks; transplant into rich, moist soil in tight blocks or double rows so the crowded plants self-blanche without tying or hilling.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun, spacing plants closely in a block rather than a single row; Golden Self-Blanching Celery was introduced in the United States in the early 1880s and became one of the most widely grown home garden celeries of its era because it needs no earthing up or wrapping to pale its stalks. Grown tightly together, the inner stalks naturally shade one another and turn a soft golden-green by fall, staying crisp and largely stringless with a clean, mild celery flavor. It matures somewhat faster than many older celery types, making it a practical choice for gardeners without a long, reliably cool season to spare. Water evenly and consistently throughout the growing period, since irregular moisture is the most common cause of stringy, bitter stalks in any celery.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into rich, evenly moist soil after frost danger passes. Redventure holds up well to cool fall weather, making it a good candidate for a second, later-season planting.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun; Redventure is a stabilized modern breeding-line celery developed by plant breeder Frank Morton in the early 1990s from a cross of the tough, strongly flavored heirloom Giant Red celery and the smoother, more tender Ventura celery. The result combines brilliant red-to-magenta stalks and luminous emerald leaves with a chewy but non-stringy texture and a more intense, concentrated celery flavor than typical green cultivars. Because the flavor and color are so pronounced, Redventure is especially well suited to soups, stocks, and braises where its stalks and leaves add both color and depth rather than being eaten raw on their own. It is notably cold-tolerant for a celery, extending the usable harvest window well into fall.

common_name: Prinz Celeriac (German Smooth-Skinned Bolt-Resistant Celery Root)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost transplant date; Prinz has notably strong bolt resistance, so it can be set out earlier under cover than most celeriac without the risk of premature flowering that cold shock triggers in less resistant varieties.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, consistently moist, very fertile soil; Prinz is a German-bred celeriac valued for producing rounded, smooth, light-skinned globes that clean up easily compared with the rougher-skinned older varieties, with dense, firm, pure white interior flesh. Its strong resistance to premature bolting makes it more forgiving of an early start under row cover or plastic than most celeriac, while it also performs reliably as a later, unprotected planting. The flavor is a clean, nutty, concentrated celery essence, equally good raw and grated into rémoulade or cooked into soups, purees, and roasts. As with all celeriac, keep the soil evenly moist throughout the long growing season and remove small side roots from the developing globe to encourage a smooth, well-formed root.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Dusky is one of the earliest classic dark-skinned hybrid eggplants to reach harvest size.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dusky is a compact hybrid eggplant that became a home-garden standard for its combination of early maturity, good disease resistance, and heavy sets of deep purple, glossy, oval-to-teardrop fruit. Fruits reach a full 8 to 9 inches while still maturing notably faster than many older large-fruited eggplants, which lets gardeners in shorter-season regions get a reliable harvest before fall cooling slows production. The dense, disease-tolerant bush habit performs well in raised beds and large containers as well as open garden rows. Pick fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm and the flesh gives slightly to gentle pressure, since fruit left to overripen turns dull, seedy, and bitter.

common_name: Clara Eggplant (Italian White Oval Hybrid Eggplant)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Clara is a vigorous, disease-tolerant Italian hybrid that yields heavily over a long harvest window.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Clara is an Italian hybrid eggplant grown for its striking, brilliantly white, oval fruit set off by a bright green calyx, giving it strong visual appeal at market and in the garden alike. The dense white flesh is mild and free of the bitterness that can affect some white-skinned types, holding its color well when cut and cooking down smoothly for baked and roasted preparations. Clara shows good tolerance to common eggplant diseases and sets fruit heavily and early relative to many other Italian-type hybrids, extending the productive harvest window in a single season. Harvest fruit at 6 to 7 inches long while the skin is still glossy and firm, since white eggplant dulls and toughens quickly once past its prime.
